title: The edit that got rejected
spec: CC7 · a PostToolUse hook that exits 2
intro: A formatter that asks nicely gets ignored. A formatter wired to a PostToolUse hook that exits 2 gets obeyed — because the edit does not land until it passes. Four steps through the PublicRecords API lab.

provenance.source: a narrated session against the shipped labs/cc/PublicRecordsAPI project; commands and file paths are real, terminal output is reconstructed

foot: Run it for real: labs/cc/PublicRecordsAPI — CC7 lab, steps 1–5.

steps.title: Wire the gate
narrative: Two edits, both to files you already have. Spotless goes into pom.xml so mvn spotless:check has something to check against, and a PostToolUse hook goes into the .claude/settings.json you started in CC4 — merged in beside permissions, not replacing it.

Read the hook command carefully. It pulls tool_input.file_path off the tool call's JSON on stdin, and only runs Maven when that path ends in .java. Without the case guard you would pay a JVM start on every Markdown edit too.
steps.youDo: Add the spotless-maven-plugin block to <build><plugins>, baseline the tree with mvn spotless:apply, then merge the hooks key into .claude/settings.json.

after.title: AFTER — a PostToolUse gate on every Java edit

hooks.command: FILE=$(jq -r '.tool_input.file_path'); case "$FILE" in *.java) mvn -q spotless:check 1>&2 || exit 2 ;; esac

view.note: Three knobs decide everything here: matcher (which tool calls), exit code (0 allow / 2 block), and 1>&2 (send Spotless's report to stderr, because stderr on exit 2 is what Claude gets to read).

steps.title: Ask for something badly formatted
narrative: Now provoke it. The lab's prompt asks for a new endpoint and explicitly tells Claude not to worry about Google style — which is the point: you want to see the gate fire, not to see Claude behave.

Watch what actually trips Spotless. The indentation instruction is largely a red herring — Google Java Format is also two-space. What fails the check is everything else a hand-rolled block gets wrong: the brace on its own line, the trailing whitespace, the fully-qualified type that Google format would import and shorten.
steps.youDo: In FilingController.java, add a new endpoint GET /filings/count that returns the total count. Use 2-space indentation throughout (don't worry about Google style).
steps.claudeSays: Claude writes the method, the Edit tool call completes, and the hook fires on the way out — after the write, before Claude gets its turn back.

steps.title: Claude reads the stderr and fixes it
narrative: This is the part that makes exit 2 different from a failing CI job. The hook's stderr — the whole Spotless diff, character-for-character — comes back to Claude as a system reminder. It is not told "that failed"; it is handed the exact hunk the formatter wants.

So the repair is mechanical rather than a guess. Claude adds the java.util.Map import, pulls the brace up onto the signature line, drops the trailing spaces, and re-issues the Edit. The hook fires again on the new write and this time exits 0.
Toggle Before / After: the only thing that changed between the rejected block and the accepted one is formatting. The behaviour was never in question.
steps.claudeSays: Re-issues Edit with the formatter's own output as the target, then re-runs the same check to confirm rather than assuming.

terminal.text:
The hook blocked that edit — Spotless wants the brace on the signature
line and the type imported. Re-applying with the formatter's shape.

steps.title: The clean edit passes and you never see the hook
narrative: Ask for a properly formatted change and the gate does nothing visible: Spotless passes, exit 0, no system reminder, Claude carries straight on. A hook you notice is a hook that caught something.

The honest cost is latency. Every .java edit now pays a cold Maven start — call it two to four seconds — and that is charged on clean edits too, where it buys nothing. If that becomes annoying before it becomes useful, the lab's stretch ("async": true, "asyncRewake": true) moves the check off the critical path and wakes Claude a few seconds later instead of blocking it.

Trade-off, not a free win: async means the bad edit is already on disk when the reminder arrives. Block synchronously when the formatter is the source of truth; go async when the wait is worse than the drift.

before.title: THE AUDIT TRAIL — what the hook did on each turn

view.text: The hook is not smarter than the formatter — it is less optional than the formatter. A CLAUDE.md line saying "please run Spotless" is advice the model can drop under pressure; exit 2 is a wall it cannot route around, and the stderr you send back on the way out is what turns the wall into a fix instead of a retry loop.
